items.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> leans on the left, tucked behind it a little <radical>cocoon</radical>, sealed tight. Nobody else knows it is there. You grew the crop in the open, then kept one seed back for yourself: <kanji>private</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Shi is the quiet one who keeps her own small field behind the house, and when anyone asks what she is growing in it she says 「<reading>し</reading>」 and closes the gate. Not rude, exactly. Whatever is in there is hers, and し is the only answer you are ever going to get.

items.mnemonic_text: A single horizontal stroke is the ground floor: one.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>ground</radical> radical is already in your head, and the <kanji>one</kanji> kanji is the very same flat line.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker called <reading>Itchy</reading> lies on the floor as flat as that single line on the ground, scratching his bites and groaning 「<reading>いち</reading>」, a lone flat line meaning <kanji form="一">one</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: Two stacked strokes count out two.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>two</radical> radical walked straight into the kanji list without changing a stroke, so the <kanji>two</kanji> kanji costs you nothing new.
items.reading_mnemonic: A clumsy waiter called <reading>Knee</reading> bangs his knee on the table and the chopsticks jump, so he hisses 「<reading>に</reading>」 and lays them back one above the other to make <kanji form="二">two</kanji>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Deep in a <radical>thicket</radical> where every other <radical>person</radical> is hidden, the only one I can still point to is <kanji>me</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Lost in that same thicket, a hiker finally crashes out into the open, hugging one soggy paperback <reading>book</reading> to his chest. When the ranger asks whose it is, all he can gasp between breaths is <reading>ぼく</reading> — mine, that one is me.
items.description: As a first-person word this is used mainly by boys and men and stays casual, so it is out of place in formal writing or when you must be very polite. It grew out of an older, humble word for a servant.

items.mnemonic_text: Three stacked strokes: one, two, three.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Copy the flat <radical>ground</radical> line, then draw it twice more above itself, and the stubby ladder of level rungs you get is <kanji>three</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cat named <reading>Sun</reading> basks on the top rung of that stubby ladder of flat lines, and you count 「<reading>さん</reading>」 as you climb up to her on rung <kanji form="三">three</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth boxing in legs that kick four ways: four.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Trapped inside a doorless <radical>enclosure</radical>, your <radical>human legs</radical> pace off all <kanji>four</kanji> of its walls before you admit there is no way out.
items.reading_mnemonic: A sheep called <reading>She</reading> is stuck in the same doorless enclosure you paced earlier, tramping its four walls on a loop. At each corner she halts and bleats <reading>し</reading> at the blank stone, waiting for a door to appear. Four corners, four bleats, still no way out.
items.description: The look-alike is 西 west. In 四 the mark inside the box is a small pair of splayed legs that hang from the top and spread downward without touching the walls. 西 is noticeably taller, and its two inner strokes stand straight up like poles fixed to the top edge.

items.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>official</radical> whose <radical>mouth</radical> is always hanging open to bark one more order is exactly the man everyone is forced to call <kanji>mister</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: That same barking official trudges up the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine. The cats swarm him and web him into a fat silk <reading>cocoon</reading> in seconds, and every command he keeps shouting from inside now comes out as a muffled <reading>くん</reading>.
items.description: Not a polite title. As a name-suffix it marks a junior, a classmate, or a young man rather than a superior. As a stand-alone word it is a familiar 'you' that can sound blunt with someone you barely know.

items.mnemonic_text: A shape crossing itself, the hand held up: five fingers.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You already met <radical>five</radical> as a radical, and the <kanji>five</kanji> kanji is that same shape with nothing added.
items.reading_mnemonic: A coach yells <reading>go</reading>, flattened to 「<reading>ご</reading>」, and you leap for a high-five, but the low ceiling traps your hand flat with all <kanji form="五">five</kanji> fingers spread.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> at the left edge, beside a hide hauled off in one sheet — all <radical>skin</radical>, no animal left. Someone walked past carrying it and is already down the road. That man you point at and cannot name: <kanji>he</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Hii is the little intake of breath you make when the man in the skin cloak goes past without a word — 「<reading>ひ</reading>」. By the time you finish it, he is round the corner. Every time you catch sight of him: ひ.

items.mnemonic_text: A little hat on two legs stands over six.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <radical>number eight</radical> standing tall, and then set a little <radical>lid</radical> right on top of it. That lid caps the eight and knocks it down two — from eight, you drop to six. The lid on top of eight always means <kanji>six</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>rock</reading> star leaps onto the tall eight, slams the little lid on its head and screams 「<reading>ろく</reading>」 as the eight sinks two notches to <kanji form="六">six</kanji>.
items.description: Means six; the basic number 6, seen everywhere from counting and prices to dates and times.

items.mnemonic_text: A slanted cross like a scythe cutting seven.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every hour you spent learning the radical <radical>seven</radical> is paid back here, because the <kanji>seven</kanji> kanji is the exact same character.
items.reading_mnemonic: The sneaky fan who <reading>cheats</reading> swats rivals with his big foam finger until its soft end curls up, and he still waves it, chanting 「<reading>しち</reading>」 for <kanji form="七">seven</kanji>.
items.description: The look-alike is 十 (ten). In 十 the crossing stroke is a straight vertical down through the center, ending pointing straight down in a clean plus. In 七 that stroke crosses higher, then bends hard right along the bottom and flicks up, so the shape leans and hooks.

items.mnemonic_text: Two strokes spreading apart like the number eight opening up.
items.meaning_mnemonic: There is no work to do on this one, since the radical <radical>eight</radical> and the <kanji>eight</kanji> kanji are one and the same character.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woodcutter swings his <reading>hatchet</reading> into the log, and as the two halves fall apart he grunts 「<reading>はち</reading>」, splitting it into the shape of <kanji form="八">eight</kanji>.
items.description: The look-alikes are 入 (enter) and 人 (person). In 人 the two strokes join in a sharp peak at the top. In 入 they meet near the top too, but the right stroke pokes up past the join. In 八 the strokes never touch, leaving an open gap at the top.

items.mnemonic_text: A hook curling back at the top of the count: nine.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>nine</radical> radical and the <kanji>nine</kanji> kanji are the same character, so this one lands in your memory for free.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman lines up a shot with a pool <reading>cue</reading> instead of a rod. The ninth ball he sinks leaps back out of the water like a hooked fish, and he shouts <reading>きゅう</reading> at the splash.
items.description: Both 九 and 力 end in a hooked stroke, but the hooks point opposite ways. In 九 the final stroke sweeps wide to the right and flicks up, leaving that side open. In 力 it drops nearly straight and hooks back to the left at the foot, so the shape stays narrow. At the top, 九 has a short slant the body crosses over, while 力 opens with a bent stroke that makes a hard corner.

items.mnemonic_text: A perfect plus sign, fingers of both hands: ten.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>ten</radical> radical and the <kanji>ten</kanji> kanji are the very same mark, so this is one you already know for free.
items.reading_mnemonic: You lay two matchsticks in a cross, one flat and one standing, then spill <reading>juice</reading> on it, and the soggy plus that means <kanji form="十">ten</kanji> fizzles out with a 「<reading>じゅう</reading>」.
items.description: 十 is a single upright stroke crossed by one flat horizontal. 千 (thousand) adds a short slash slanting in above that cross. 七 (seven) has no upright at all: one stroke bends and hooks up to the right beneath a high, tilted bar.

items.mnemonic_text: One (一) over a white (白) sheet counted a hundred times.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>one</radical> stroke sits on top of a blinding <radical>white</radical> light bulb. The light is so bright the stroke multiplies into copies of itself. Soon there are exactly a <kanji>hundred</kanji> strokes glowing on the ceiling.
items.reading_mnemonic: Staring into the blinding white bulb gives you a <reading>hiccup</reading>, and each 「<reading>ひゃく</reading>」 copies the stroke on top until a <kanji form="百">hundred</kanji> of them glow on the ceiling.
items.description: 百 is 白 with one extra stroke on top. 白 caps its box with a small flick; 百 turns that cap into a full-width horizontal bar.

items.mnemonic_text: A slash over ten (十) multiplies it into a thousand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Drop a single <radical>slash</radical> across your tally of <radical>ten</radical> and the whole count suddenly jumps to a <kanji>thousand</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at that smeared tally wall in the school hallway, Sei counts the marks, gives up, and decides to just <reading>send</reading> the whole impossible number through as one lump sum. It goes as <reading>せん</reading>, a flat thousand that nobody is ever going to recount.
items.description: 千 opens with a slash from the upper right, above one horizontal and the upright. 十 (ten) is that shape without the slash. 午 (noon) keeps the slash but runs two horizontals. 干 (dry or shield) has two horizontals as well, but a flat straight top instead of a slash.

items.mnemonic_text: A single hooked mark standing for a whole ten thousand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>ten thousand</radical> radical and the <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> kanji are the same, so this is one review you get for nothing.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Manny</reading> the deli clerk chases the ticket rolling from the machine down to the floor, reads the number on it, and sighs 「<reading>まん</reading>」, because it says <kanji form="万">ten thousand</kanji>.
items.description: The look-alike 方 (direction / person) puts a short slanted stroke above its first horizontal line; 'ten thousand' has no stroke there. Its last stroke also drops in a near-straight squarish leg, where 'ten thousand' swings that stroke out in one wide sweep.

items.mnemonic_text: A boxed shape holding the round yen coin.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>stick</radical> pinned at one end to the <radical>ground</radical> and swung all the way around the inside of a <radical>wide box</radical> scratches out the round coin you spend as one <kanji>yen</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The monk <reading>Zen</reading> pins the stick to the ground and swings it round inside the wide box, murmuring 「<reading>えん</reading>」 as the scratched circle becomes one <kanji form="円">yen</kanji> coin.

items.mnemonic_text: A window with a line: the sun rising to mark the day.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Because the <radical>sun</radical> radical and the <kanji>day</kanji> kanji are the very same character, every hour you spent learning radicals is quietly paying you back here.
items.reading_mnemonic: A ranger called <reading>Neech</reading> squints through the tall barred window as the sun rises behind the glass, and mutters 「<reading>にち</reading>」, because another <kanji form="日">day</kanji> has started.
items.description: The look-alike 白 (white) is this same barred box with one extra short stroke flicked onto the top; take that flick away and you are back to 'day'. The look-alike 目 (eye) is a taller box with two bars across the middle instead of one, stacking three sections where 'day' has only two.

items.mnemonic_text: A crescent with two lines: the moon marking each month.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>moon</radical> radical and the <kanji>month</kanji> kanji are the same character, which makes sense once you remember a month is just one lap of the moon.
items.reading_mnemonic: Once a month the night janitor at Sei's school, a man called <reading>Getz</reading>, mops the echoing hallway by the light of the full moon. The moonlight through the tall windows lights up every streak he missed, so he groans <reading>げつ</reading> and mops the whole floor over again.

items.mnemonic_text: A person with sparks flying off each side: fire.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You already know the <radical>fire</radical> radical, and the <kanji>fire</kanji> kanji is that same upright log with sparks flicking off both sides.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, lands on the upright log and gives one <reading>caw</reading>, and her 「<reading>か</reading>」 spits two sparks off its sides and sets the log on <kanji form="火">fire</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: Streams splashing out from a central flow: water.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>water</radical> radical and the <kanji>water</kanji> kanji are the exact same splash, one central stream with two trickles flying off, frozen mid-air.
items.reading_mnemonic: A big white swan has claimed the riverbank, and every time someone kneels to wash clothes she flaps up and drags a hard <reading>sweep</reading> of spray across their back. You stand there soaked and dripping. That cold slap of river water off her wings is the sound <reading>すい</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: A trunk with roots and branches: a tree.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Here the <radical>tree</radical> radical and the <kanji>tree</kanji> kanji line up stroke for stroke, trunk, spreading branch, and roots gripping the soil.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki, the tree spirit, giggles inside her old oak whenever the wind blows, until a hiker carves his initials into her bark. She leans out of the trunk to <reading>mock</reading> him, repeating every word he says in a flat little voice. He drops the knife and runs, her <reading>もく</reading> chasing him down the trail.
items.description: The look-alike 本 (book / origin) is this same tree with one extra short bar across the foot of the trunk, just above where the roots split. 木 leaves that space clean. A low bar on the trunk means 本, not 木.

items.mnemonic_text: A roof over a mountain of buried gold and money.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>gold</radical> radical and the <kanji>gold</kanji> kanji are the very same character, which also came to mean money because for centuries gold coins were exactly what people paid with.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tiny <reading>king</reading> sits under the little roof guarding the two nuggets on their stand, and announces 「<reading>きん</reading>」 each time he polishes his <kanji form="金">gold</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: A cross pushed into the ground: earth and soil.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You met this shape already as the <radical>earth</radical> radical, and the <kanji>earth</kanji> kanji is the very same character, used just as happily for the loose soil that earth breaks down into.
items.reading_mnemonic: A gardener hammers the wooden signpost into the flat ground with a deep 「<reading>ど</reading>」, and the soft <kanji form="土">earth</kanji> squishes up around it like <reading>dough</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: Three peaks rising up: a mountain range.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This one is a freebie, since the <radical>mountain</radical> radical and the <kanji>mountain</kanji> kanji are the exact same character.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker slogs up the steep mountain trail toward the lone vending machine at the top. Right as she reaches the summit the <reading>sun</reading> clears the ridge and blinds her, and all she can manage is <reading>さん</reading> before feeding in her coins.

items.mnemonic_text: Three flowing lines of a running river.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>river</radical> radical and the <kanji>river</kanji> kanji are the same character, drawn as the same three flowing strokes every single time.
items.reading_mnemonic: A courier crouches at the riverbank, certain the fastest way to <reading>send</reading> a parcel across is to float it. The current takes it the instant it touches the water and skims it away downstream, hissing <reading>せん</reading> over the shallows.

items.mnemonic_text: A person (大) with a line above their head: the heavens.
items.meaning_mnemonic: One flat <radical>ground</radical> line laid above the arms of the <radical>big</radical> outstretched person turns everything higher than it into <kanji>heaven</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Out on the school sports field, the gym teacher the kids call <reading>Ten</reading> makes the whole class lie flat on the ground. Arms flung out wide, faces up at the open sky, nobody moves. He walks the rows counting slowly, and the drill ends when he reaches <reading>てん</reading>.
items.description: The one to watch is 大, meaning big. 天 has two horizontal strokes stacked at the top, while 大 has just the single crossbar for the arms. That short top line is the whole difference.

items.mnemonic_text: Steam rising with an X inside: the invisible energy or mood.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A field's <kanji>spirit</kanji> is the <radical>steam</radical> that lifts off the blades the morning after you <radical>mow</radical> them down to stubble.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit climbs out of her old oak beside the field you just mowed. Warm steam curls off the stubble and tickles her until she cannot stop giggling, a thin <reading>き</reading> sound like a tiny <reading>key</reading> scraping in a lock. She rides the vapour up and vanishes into the cold.

items.mnemonic_text: Grass on top of a person changing (化): a blooming flower.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When ordinary <radical>grass</radical> gets tired of being green and <radical>change</radical>s its top into colour, what stands there is a <kanji>flower</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, lets out a <reading>caw</reading> over the green grass, and her hot 「<reading>か</reading>」 scorches each blade's tip into red and gold until it stands as a <kanji form="花">flower</kanji>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Words</radical> stand on the left, on the right an <radical>old bird</radical> with its head cocked, waiting. You have talked for ten minutes and the bird still cannot tell which person you mean. It asks the only question left: <kanji>who</kanji>?
items.reading_mnemonic: Sui is the owl who works the gate. She leans down, blinks once, and hoots 「<reading>すい</reading>」, which in owl means name, please. Nobody gets past her without answering it. すい, すい, until you say who you are.

items.mnemonic_text: A mark sitting on top of a line: up and above.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mossy shrine steps, the tortoise's <radical>divination</radical> crack rises from the flat <radical>ground</radical> line with everything it has to say pointing <kanji>up</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Joe the window washer hangs in his cradle above the shrine roof, polishing the top of the great bell. When Grandma Kane calls to ask where he is, the only answer that floats down is <reading>じょう</reading>, the one direction he ever points. He says it like the name <reading>Joe</reading>, stretched long.

items.mnemonic_text: A mark hanging under a line: down and below.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hang the tortoise's <radical>divination</radical> mark off the underside of the <radical>ground</radical> line and it dangles <kanji>down</kanji> into the dark where no one reads it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, slips under the ground line and huffs a small flame with a 「<reading>か</reading>」 <reading>caw</reading> to read the divination mark dangling <kanji form="下">down</kanji> there in the dark.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Faced with a <radical>person</radical> who swears they <radical>can</radical> do absolutely anything, the only question left to ask is <kanji>what</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line outside Koichi's konbini and brags he can fix any broken machine. You point at the smoking till and ask <reading>か</reading>, meaning which part is even fixable. He just puffs a little flame and gives his only reply, a flat <reading>caw</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: A box speared straight through the middle.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>stick</radical> shoved straight down through a wide <radical>mouth</radical> stops dead at the exact <kanji>middle</kanji>, pinning everything trapped in there.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chuu, the loyal mouse, will not budge from the dead center of that speared mouth, and each time you try to lift him off he just squeaks <reading>ちゅう</reading> and grips the stick harder. He would <reading>chew</reading> straight through it before he let anyone take his spot in the middle.

items.mnemonic_text: A person stretching arms and legs out wide: big.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Here is one that costs you nothing, since the <radical>big</radical> radical, arms and legs flung wide, is already the finished <kanji>big</kanji> kanji.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Dai</reading>, the giant baby, flings his arms wide and plants his legs far apart to show how <kanji form="大">big</kanji> his lost bottle was, bellowing 「<reading>だい</reading>」 the whole time.
items.description: The look-alikes are 太 (thick), 天 (heaven), and 犬 (dog). All four are the same wide-armed figure with splayed legs. 大 has nothing added. 太 adds one short dot low between the legs. 天 lays a long flat stroke across the very top, above the arms. That top stroke is longer than the arm stroke. 犬 adds one small dot high on the right, near the arm. Any extra mark means it is not 大.

items.mnemonic_text: A tiny hook with two small dots: small.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You get this one free, because the <radical>small</radical> radical you already know is the <kanji>small</kanji> kanji unchanged, right down to the two fingers pinching that speck.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, pinches the one tiny seed between two hands for his big <reading>show</reading>, crying 「<reading>しょう</reading>」 to reveal just how <kanji form="小">small</kanji> it is.
items.description: The look-alike is 少, meaning few or little. It is this kanji with one stroke added: a short slanting stroke laid over the top right, making four strokes instead of three. If the centre hook and its two side marks stand alone with nothing above them, it is small; if a stray diagonal caps the top, it is few.

items.mnemonic_text: A hand over a craftsman's tool, held in the left hand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your flat <radical>left hand</radical> exists to hold the <radical>construction</radical> girder still while your other hand does the bolting, so <kanji>left</kanji> just means the bracing hand.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sara steadies the construction beam with her left hand, exactly as that hand is built to do, and drives the saw with her right. Every stroke drags a dry <reading>さ</reading> out of the plank, the flat sound of a <reading>saw</reading> in soft pine. She keeps going until the whole site is ankle deep in sawdust.
items.description: The look-alike is 右, meaning right. Both share the flat left-hand stroke across the top; the giveaway sits underneath, where left carries the construction beam and right holds a small closed box instead. In left the horizontal top stroke is the long one, while in right the slanting stroke is longer and the horizontal stays short.

items.mnemonic_text: A hand over a mouth, the right hand that feeds you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Once your <radical>left hand</radical> is busy holding the bowl, the only hand free to lift food to your <radical>mouth</radical> is your <kanji>right</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A fisherman named <reading>Woo</reading> eats his lunch at the riverbank one-handed, his left hand still gripping the oar, and his clumsy right keeps dropping rice down his shirt until he lets out a long <reading>う</reading>. Every lost mouthful earns another flat <reading>う</reading>.
items.description: The look-alikes are 左 (left) and 石 (stone). All three place a shape beneath a hand-like top. In 右 that top is a short slant crossing a short flat stroke, with 口 right under it. 左 keeps the same top. Its lower part is a narrow shape with a flat foot, not a closed box. 石 keeps the 口 underneath. Its top stroke stretches into one long flat overhang with a square corner, like a cliff.

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) tangled in a tree (木): sunrise in the east.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <radical>sun</radical> rising and getting tangled in the branches of a <radical>tree</radical> on the horizon. You see the sun caught right behind that tree first thing in the morning — and the sun always comes up in the east. Sun plus tree, hung together at dawn: that's <kanji>east</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker faces the sunrise and lets out a long, tired yawn — a huge "<reading>とう</reading>" that echoes down the slope. Every morning she climbs to greet the east with that same sleepy とう.

items.mnemonic_text: A bird settling into its nest as the sun sets in the west.
items.meaning_mnemonic: No new work here, because the <radical>west</radical> radical, that sun climbing down into its crate for the night, is the <kanji>west</kanji> kanji with not one stroke moved.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the school, when the teacher asks which way the sun goes down, Sei's hand is up before anyone has even finished hearing the question. Too pleased with himself to wait his turn, he leans back and says <reading>せい</reading>. It is the right answer, because that is the sound you <reading>say</reading> for west.
items.description: The look-alike is 四, meaning four. West has a separate horizontal lid across the very top that pokes out past the sides, and the two upright strokes inside rise up to meet it. Four is a plain sealed rectangle with a flat top and no overhang, and its two inner strokes curl apart at the bottom without touching the top.

items.mnemonic_text: A warm shelter facing the sunny south.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two <radical>horns</radical> poke out of a <radical>wide box</radical> lashed to the only wall that stays <radical>dry</radical> and warm through <radical>ten</radical> winters, and a wall like that faces <kanji>south</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Nan sets her deck chair against the south wall of the barn each morning, beside the old crate with the horns poking out. Ask why she never sits on the shady north side and she grumbles that it gets <reading>なん</reading> of the afternoon sun, dragging the word out as she tips her hat down. Everyone just calls her <reading>Nan</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: Two people back to back turning away from the cold north.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Here is one that comes free, because the <radical>north</radical> radical and the <kanji>north</kanji> kanji are the very same character, learned once and counted twice.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the frozen riverbank, two skaters stand back to back and guard the same net. Every time the puck clangs off the post they both bark <reading>ほく</reading>, the flat grunt a rink announcer makes yelling <reading>hockey</reading> into a dead microphone.

items.mnemonic_text: Evening (夕) plus divination: reading fortunes outside.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A tortoise doing <radical>divination</radical> in the fading <radical>evening</radical> light has to shuffle <kanji>outside</kanji> to catch the last of the sun on its cracked shell.
items.reading_mnemonic: Out behind Grandma Kane's shrine at dusk, a fortune-telling guy keeps flipping his tortoise shell for one more reading. Each blank answer drags a long <reading>がい</reading> out of him, the groan a worn-out <reading>guy</reading> makes when the cards say wait.

items.mnemonic_text: A blade cutting the way forward, in front of you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A cow lowers its <radical>horns</radical> to the <radical>ground</radical> to guard the <radical>knife</radical> it dropped, so anyone crossing the yard by <radical>moon</radical>light has to freeze right in <kanji>front</kanji> of it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Long before sunrise, a monk sweeps the gravel yard out front and bows to the last of the moon. The other monks call him <reading>Zen</reading> because, whatever the hour, he is already there, and he answers to <reading>ぜん</reading> without looking up.

items.mnemonic_text: A small step trailing behind: after and behind.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Each <radical>step</radical> you take drags a <radical>trailing foot</radical> caught on a <radical>tiny thread</radical>, so that foot always lands a beat <kanji>behind</kanji> the rest of you.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the school sports field, a gopher lines up for the relay with a thread off his own shoe wound round his back foot. The starter yells <reading>ご</reading> to make the runners <reading>go</reading>, and the gopher spends the entire lap one step behind, picking at the knot.

items.mnemonic_text: A marker at the top of the day: noon.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Held straight overhead at <kanji>noon</kanji>, a bone-<radical>dry</radical> shield throws almost no shadow, just one thin <radical>slash</radical>, because the sun is standing directly above it.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the school sports field, a gopher called <reading>Gordon</reading> only surfaces at noon, when the sun sits straight overhead and not one shadow falls to warn him. The moment the lunch bell blares <reading>ご</reading>, he bolts across the bright grass for the echoing hallways.
items.description: Two kanji crowd the same outline. 千, thousand, carries just one horizontal bar where noon stacks two, and it opens with a short flat tick instead of noon's longer left-falling slash. 牛, cow, is the nearer miss: its centre post pushes up through the top stroke, while noon's vertical stops flush against a slanted top and never breaks above it.

items.mnemonic_text: A tree (木) with a line marking its root: the origin, a book.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>tree</radical> standing tall, with the <radical>ground</radical> drawn as one flat line across its trunk — right where the roots meet the soil. That line marks the tree's own origin. Press pages flat from that origin, and you have a <kanji>book</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A bear hunting <reading>honey</reading> claws the tall tree right where its roots meet the soil, grunting 「<reading>ほん</reading>」, and the bark peels off in flat pages, a <kanji form="本">book</kanji> from its origin.
items.description: 本 is 木 with one extra stroke: a short horizontal laid across the lower trunk. Nothing else changes, so that little bar down at the base is the only thing to look for.

items.mnemonic_text: Two legs walking: a person.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Knowing your radicals pays off here, because the <radical>person</radical> radical is the <kanji>person</kanji> kanji with nothing added and nothing changed.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Jin</reading>, the friendly giant, takes one slow step, one leg planted and the other swinging forward, and each stride booms 「<reading>じん</reading>」, a walking <kanji form="人">person</kanji> the size of a hill.
items.description: The look-alikes are 入 (enter) and 八 (eight). In 人 the two strokes join in a sharp peak at the top with nothing poking out above the join. In 入 they meet near the top too, but the right stroke pushes up past the join like a small flag. In 八 the two strokes never touch, leaving an open gap at the top and spreading apart like a fan.

items.mnemonic_text: A figure kneeling gracefully: a woman.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You get the <kanji>woman</kanji> kanji for free today, since it is the same <radical>woman</radical> radical you already practised, shape and meaning untouched.
items.reading_mnemonic: A dancer called <reading>Jo</reading> crosses one leg over the other and swings her arms wide, humming 「<reading>じょ</reading>」 as she spins, a <kanji form="女">woman</kanji> in the middle of her dance.

items.mnemonic_text: Power (力) worked in the rice field (田): a working man.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>rice field</radical> stretching out under the sun, and the one person out there doing the heavy lifting. He bends his arm, flexes his <radical>power</radical>, and drags the plow across the paddies all day. Someone with that much power working the rice field — that's the <kanji>man</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The man out in the field takes a break and starts pounding out a rhythm on his empty water bucket: <reading>だん</reading>, だん, だん. Every man on the trail can hear that drumbeat and grins.

items.mnemonic_text: A swaddled baby with arms out: a child.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This <kanji>child</kanji> kanji is a gift you already own, the <radical>child</radical> radical exactly as you learned it, without a single stroke changed.
items.reading_mnemonic: The <kanji form="子">child</kanji> runs at you wrapped in a blanket with arms thrown wide for a hug, squealing so loud you put a finger to your lips and <reading>shush</reading> 「<reading>し</reading>」 into the hug.

items.mnemonic_text: An upright frame with pupils inside: an eye.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing new to memorise here, because the <kanji>eye</kanji> kanji is simply the <radical>eye</radical> radical you have already seen, identical in shape and meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Smoke</reading> drifts into the sideways box staring back at you, the eyelid snaps shut over both lines of pupil, and it splutters 「<reading>もく</reading>」, one sore <kanji form="目">eye</kanji>.
items.description: The look-alikes are 日 (day or sun) and 自 (self). 目 has three lines inside its upright box, splitting it into four stacked compartments. 日 has only one line across the middle, leaving just two. 自 is the same box as 目 but with a short slanted stroke added on top, like a finger pointing at your own nose.

items.mnemonic_text: A dangling shape on the side of the head: an ear.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Good news for once, the <radical>ear</radical> radical you already know and the <kanji>ear</kanji> kanji are the very same character.
items.reading_mnemonic: A gnat buzzes into the folds of the tall rim on the side of your head, and you yelp a startled <reading>gee</reading>, 「<reading>じ</reading>」, slapping your own <kanji form="耳">ear</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: An open square: a mouth.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This one is a freebie, because the <radical>mouth</radical> radical you already know is the whole <kanji>mouth</kanji> kanji, with nothing added.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, stretches his <kanji form="口">mouth</kanji> into a square yawn, four lips wide, then tips hot <reading>cocoa</reading> into the hole and yelps 「<reading>こう</reading>」.

items.mnemonic_text: Fingers and a wrist branching out: a hand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This one is free if you learned your radicals well, because the <radical>hand</radical> radical and the <kanji>hand</kanji> kanji are one and the same character.
items.reading_mnemonic: A pigeon lands on the open palm of old <reading>Shoo</reading>, so he spreads his fingers wide, flaps that whole <kanji form="手">hand</kanji> at it and hisses 「<reading>しゅ</reading>」 until it flies off.

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth over stopping legs: a foot that carries you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> sits on top of a pair of legs. The legs have skidded to a halt — they are <radical>stopping</radical> hard. They end in one part: a <radical>foot</radical>. That's your <kanji>foot</kanji>, your leg, plenty to stand on.
items.reading_mnemonic: The walking mouth named <reading>Sock</reading> skids to such a hard stop that the sock flies off its <kanji form="足">foot</kanji>, and it yelps 「<reading>そく</reading>」 at its bare toes.
items.description: Means foot, leg, or to suffice/be enough; shows up in words for body parts and in verbs about having sufficient amounts.

items.mnemonic_text: A flexed arm pushing: power and strength.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>power</radical> radical and the <kanji>power</kanji> kanji are the same character, and strength is just that same power once you can feel it straining in your muscles.
items.reading_mnemonic: The weightlifter <reading>Rocky</reading> bends one arm at the elbow until the muscle bulges hard as a rock, and grunts 「<reading>りょく</reading>」 at all that <kanji form="力">power</kanji>.
items.description: The one to watch is 九, 'nine'. In 力 the long stroke drops straight down the right side and ends in a small hook curling to the left. In 九 that stroke swings out wide to the right and finishes with a hook low on the right, and its first stroke pokes out past the top-left corner.

items.mnemonic_text: A sprout pushing up from the ground: life and birth.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing new here, the <radical>life</radical> radical and the <kanji>life</kanji> kanji are one character, and it also covers birth because birth is just where a life begins.
items.reading_mnemonic: In a hallway at Sei's school, the teacher barely finishes asking what that first shoot through the soil stands for. Sei's hand is already up, uniform crease-perfect, and she <reading>says</reading> <reading>せい</reading> before anyone else draws breath. She looks quietly smug about beating the whole class to it.

items.mnemonic_text: In the evening (夕) you call out a mouth's (口) name.
items.meaning_mnemonic: In the <radical>evening</radical> nobody can see your face, so your <radical>mouth</radical> has to give your <kanji>name</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: In the dark evening nobody can see <reading>May</reading>'s face, so her mouth calls 「<reading>めい</reading>」 out into the night to tell everyone her <kanji form="名">name</kanji>.
items.description: 名 and 多 both start with the same slanted three-stroke piece. 名 finishes with a small closed box beneath it. 多 repeats that slanted piece a second time instead, so it is one shape stacked twice.

items.mnemonic_text: A person carrying grain across one full year.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>year</kanji> that passes, you scratch one more <radical>chevron</radical> into the sun-<radical>dry</radical> shield-board you keep staked in the <radical>ground</radical> beside the gate.
items.reading_mnemonic: By the gate at Grandma Kane's shrine stands that scratched tally board, and a fat cat called <reading>Nan</reading> sharpens her claws on it every day. Each New Year, Grandma adds a fresh notch, the cat complains about the dulled edge, and her long flat meow drags out as <reading>ねん</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) at the temple (寺) marks the hour.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> crossing the <radical>Buddhist temple</radical> roof is how the whole village used to tell the <kanji>time</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Old monk <reading>Jiro</reading> watches the sun cross the temple roof and shouts 「<reading>じ</reading>」 down to the village each time it passes a beam, so everyone knows the <kanji form="時">time</kanji>.
items.description: Means time or hour, and shows up everywhere you talk about clock time and telling the hour.

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) seen through a gate (門): the space in between.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>gate</radical> with its two swinging doors thrown open. Right in the gap between them, the <radical>sun</radical> is hanging low, filling the opening with light. That sliver of sun caught in the gate is the space between things — an interval, the gap <kanji>between</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A guard named Kan stands watch in that gateway, timing exactly how long the sun lingers in the gap. Every time the interval passes he shouts "<reading>かん</reading>!" and slams one door shut.
items.description: 間 and 聞 are the same gate frame with different contents. 間 sets 日, the sun, inside the gateway. 聞 stands an ear there instead. What is framed by the gate settles it every time.

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) with wings and birds: naming each day of the week.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>weekday</kanji> is any <radical>day</radical> that begins when a startled <radical>pheasant</radical> shoots straight up, lands right back down, and screeches until you leave for work.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every <kanji form="曜">weekday</kanji> the startled pheasant screeches at the tired commuter <reading>Yo</reading>, and he grunts a flat 「<reading>よう</reading>」 back at it as he leaves for work.
items.description: The gloss 'weekday' really covers the whole week, weekend included; it means 'day of the week'. You will meet this kanji almost only inside those day names and almost nowhere else.

items.mnemonic_text: A roof over a moment held in the hand: now.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>now</radical> radical is the <kanji>now</kanji> kanji with nothing changed, so this one is a free point if you learned your radicals.
items.reading_mnemonic: The giant arrow tip hangs in the air over the coin, and when <reading>Conk</reading> the raccoon dawdles, it drops and bonks his head with a 「<reading>こん</reading>」: pick it up <kanji form="今">now</kanji>!
items.description: The look-alike is 会, 'meet'. Both wear the same wide peaked lid on top. Beneath the lid, 今 keeps almost nothing: a short flat dash above one small hooked stroke. 会 fills that space with a full horizontal line and a small angled shape sitting under it. Crowded underneath means 会; nearly empty with only a tiny tail means 今.

items.mnemonic_text: Making a lap around the calendar road: one week.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>week</kanji> is just how long it takes to <radical>advance</radical> the whole way around the <radical>circumference</radical> of the calendar and trip back over your own Monday footprints.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei jogs one lap of the school field every morning for a week, and by the seventh her right shoe's sole has peeled clean off from tracing the same circle. She lifts the flapping <reading>shoe</reading> and groans <reading>しゅう</reading>, the wet slap it makes on the track. Seven laps, one dead <reading>しゅう</reading>, one week gone.

items.mnemonic_text: A person over a mother figure repeating every time.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Adding an angled <radical>chevron</radical> across the <radical>do not</radical> bar turns a single ban into one that covers <kanji>every</kanji> object in the room.
items.reading_mnemonic: The toddler <reading>My</reading> grabs at each toy in the room shouting 「<reading>まい</reading>」, but the chevron ban across the door covers <kanji form="毎">every</kanji> object, so she gets none.

items.mnemonic_text: A shape split evenly down the middle: half.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A shape with a pair of <radical>horns</radical> above a <radical>cross</radical>, sliced straight down to the <radical>ground</radical>, leaves each side holding exactly one <kanji>half</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind the counter at Koichi's konbini, <reading>Han</reading> the half-and-half chef lifts every onigiri off the shelf and slices it clean down the middle before he will ring it up. Ask him why, and he just holds up the two matching pieces and says his own name, <reading>はん</reading>.
items.description: Keep this apart from 羊, sheep, which lines up three horizontal bars beneath its horns and lets its centre stroke stop at the lowest bar. Half has only two bars, and its centre stroke drives straight through the bottom one and pokes out underneath.

items.mnemonic_text: A sword (刀) dividing something into parts and minutes.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The woodcutter prises a chipped <radical>sword</radical> out of its frozen rice cake and wipes it clean. She gives it one job: split a log. It comes down clean, and the two halves lean apart into a fresh <radical>eight</radical>. One <kanji>minute</kanji>, one cut, and the sword finally earns its keep.
items.reading_mnemonic: The woodcutter, sawdust in her eyebrows, times herself at one log a minute and calls it the most <reading>fun</reading> you can have before breakfast. The sword, back in her hands and still chipped, snorts <reading>ふん</reading> — it was the one doing all the work.

items.mnemonic_text: A child (子) under a roof of scattered ideas: study.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>small</radical> <radical>child</radical> under a <radical>cover</radical> with nothing to do but turn pages is going to <kanji>study</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The small child under the cover can only <reading>gawk</reading> at page after page, muttering 「<reading>がく</reading>」, since under there all he can do is <kanji form="学">study</kanji>.
items.description: Means study or learning; a very common kanji that shows up in words for student, school, and academic subjects.

items.mnemonic_text: A tree (木) crossed with mingling students: a school.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Plant a <radical>tree</radical> along each path so hundreds of kids <radical>mingle</radical> in the shade where the walkways cross, and you have built a <kanji>school</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi the konbini king becomes the <kanji form="校">school</kanji> <reading>coach</reading>, blowing his whistle under the tree where the paths cross and barking 「<reading>こう</reading>」 at the kids who mingle in its shade.

items.mnemonic_text: A person stepping ahead of the rest: previous and first.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The one whose striding <radical>human legs</radical> have already worn a diagonal <radical>slash</radical> of path into the bare <radical>earth</radical> is the one out <kanji>ahead</kanji> of us.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the steep mountain trail, a hiker called <reading>Sen</reading> stays exactly one switchback in front of you the whole climb, so all you ever catch is her fresh bootprints in the mud. Shout up to ask how much farther, and the only word that drifts back down is <reading>せん</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: Speech (言) with a mouth counting to five (五): words and language.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A waterfall of <radical>speech</radical> pours down into a waiting <radical>mouth</radical> below. The mouth swallows every word whole without chewing once. Stuffed with so many words, it finally speaks a whole <kanji>language</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A chatty man named <reading>Go</reading> stands under the waterfall of speech with his mouth wide open, gulping 「<reading>ご</reading>」 after every word until he can speak a whole <kanji form="語">language</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: Speech (言) plus a tongue (舌): telling a story.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> releasing stacked lines of <radical>speech</radical> leans in close, and right beside it a <radical>tongue</radical> sticks out of a mouth, wagging nonstop. Put the speech next to the busy tongue and you've got someone who just won't stop talking, spinning story after <kanji>story</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Wanda the storyteller loves an audience, so she waves both hands and calls out "<reading>わ</reading>!" every time she starts a new tale. That little "わ" is her signal that another long talk is about to begin.
items.description: Means talk or story; shows up in everyday words for speaking, conversation, and telephone.

items.mnemonic_text: Words (言) sold (売) to your eyes: reading.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Somebody has to <radical>sell</radical> you the <radical>words</radical> before you can sit down anywhere and <kanji>read</kanji> them.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reader you find hunched over those lines of speech is a poison-pen critic, and you nickname her Doku (<reading>どく</reading>) because every review she reads she then tears apart. Watch her read a page and you can practically see the どく venom drip off her pen.

items.mnemonic_text: A brush (聿) laid over a sunny page: writing.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>brush</radical> moving all <radical>day</radical> with nothing to show for it but marks means somebody had to <kanji>write</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Little <reading>Shorty</reading> the scribe drags his brush across the page all day, grunting 「<reading>しょ</reading>」 at every mark, because all anyone hired him to do is <kanji form="書">write</kanji>.
items.description: Means "write"; shows up in words about writing, documents, and books, like 書く (to write).

items.mnemonic_text: An ear (耳) inside the gate (門): listening for who is there.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>ear</radical> pressed to the crack in the <radical>gate</radical> is there for one reason, which is to <kanji>hear</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Mon-Bun, the scholarly rabbit twins, press their ears to the gate to hear you ask a question. They immediately start arguing about the answer. "<reading>ぶん</reading>!" they squeak in unison. Those two never agree on anything they overhear.
items.description: 聞 and 間 are the same gate frame with different things standing inside it. 聞 puts 耳, an ear, in the gateway. 間 frames the sun there instead. What the gate contains is the whole difference.

items.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Morning</kanji> is the one stretch of the day when the striped light of <radical>sunrise</radical> is already up while the <radical>moon</radical> still hangs in the window.
items.reading_mnemonic: Cho, the rooster who always oversleeps, finally crows <reading>ちょう</reading> from the fence rail just as the last of the moonlight fades. Every house on the mountain trail wakes to that one lazy <reading>Cho</reading>. It is the sound that tells you the day has already started.
items.description: Beyond the daily sense, 朝 also names a dynasty or imperial court, and it turns up in words for a ruling era or reigning house. At this level only morning is tested.

items.mnemonic_text: A crossroads where you choose to go.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You already met the <radical>going</radical> radical, and the kanji for <kanji>go</kanji> is that same crossroads with not one stroke added, so take the free point.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi the konbini king stands at the crossroads handing each walker a <reading>coupon</reading> and barking 「<reading>こう</reading>」, so they pick a road, left or right, and <kanji form="行">go</kanji>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Daytime</kanji> is just the distance a <radical>ruler</radical> measures upward from the <radical>daybreak</radical> line to wherever the sun has climbed by now.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chuu, the loyal mouse with the tiny topknot, guards the sundial for the whole bright stretch of the day. When the shadow shrinks to nothing, he marks the middle of it with one proud <reading>ちゅう</reading>. That squeak is really just him biting a rice cracker, a single loud <reading>chew</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: A tree of grain drawing people to come.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When a single grain of <radical>rice</radical> bursts apart and the pieces scatter over the flat <radical>ground</radical>, a whole crop is about to <kanji>come</kanji> up where each one landed.
items.reading_mnemonic: A farmer named <reading>Rye</reading> kneels on the flat ground where the burst rice grain scattered, whispering 「<reading>らい</reading>」 to each piece until a whole crop starts to <kanji form="来">come</kanji> up.
items.description: The look-alike is 米, 'rice', the piece tucked inside this kanji too. 米 turns on one central crossing point with four loose dashes flung to the corners and nothing across the top. 来 lays a flat line along its top and a short crossbar through the middle, so its centre reads like a ladder, not an X. A flat roof on top means 来; two loose dots mean 米.

items.mnemonic_text: A broom and a stop: sweeping up and returning home.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Putting down the <radical>knife</radical> and picking up the <radical>sweeper</radical> is what you do the hour you <kanji>return</kanji> home.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Kiki</reading> the tree spirit drops her knife by the door and grabs the sweeper with a happy 「<reading>き</reading>」 the moment she <kanji form="帰">return</kanji>s home.
items.description: Means "return," as in going or coming back home; the core kanji in the verb 帰る, to return.

items.mnemonic_text: Two mountains stacked, something pushing out.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>exit</kanji> a lidless <radical>open box</radical>, you have to stack loose rocks into a <radical>mountain</radical> and climb out over its top.
items.reading_mnemonic: Stuck in the lidless box, the hiker <reading>Shoots</reading> piles rocks into a mountain, then <reading>shoots</reading> out over its top yelling 「<reading>しゅつ</reading>」 as she makes her <kanji form="出">exit</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: A person ducking under a doorway to enter.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>enter</radical> radical and the <kanji>enter</kanji> kanji are the same character, so this is one you already know if you learned your radicals well.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi fits a brand-<reading>new</reading> automatic door at the konbini, and it reads people so eagerly that the moment a customer leans in to enter, it snaps wide and a recorded voice sings <reading>にゅう</reading>. Now a line of schoolkids leans in and back out by the onigiri shelf, setting it off over and over.
items.description: 入, 人, and 八 are the same two strokes in three arrangements. In 入 they overlap near the top, so the left stroke pokes out past the join. In 人 they meet at one clean point with nothing sticking up above it. In 八 the two strokes never touch at all, splayed apart with a gap at the top.

items.mnemonic_text: An eye (目) on legs going out to see.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take an <radical>eye</radical> (目) and stand it up on a pair of <radical>human legs</radical> (儿), and suddenly it can <radical>see</radical> and walk around anywhere it wants. Where does an eye on legs go? Out into the world, to look at everything. So this is what it means to <kanji>see</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Ken</reading> the sword-collecting dog chases the walking eye on legs around the yard, barking 「<reading>けん</reading>」, because he wants it to <kanji form="見">see</kanji> his newest sword.
items.description: Means "see" and is the base of the common verb 見る (to see/look); it shows up constantly in everyday words about looking and watching.

items.mnemonic_text: A foot planted firmly: stop.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>stop</radical> radical and the <kanji>stop</kanji> kanji are identical in shape and meaning, so knowing your radicals well just handed you this one for free.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Sheila</reading> plants her foot flat on the ground, heel and toes dug in, and hisses 「<reading>し</reading>」 at anyone who tries to push her on, because that foot has come to a <kanji form="止">stop</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: A person standing on the ground line: to stand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>stand</radical> radical and the <kanji>stand</kanji> kanji are the very same shape and sense, so this one costs you nothing new.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the sports field the coach at Sei's school makes the whole class stand at attention until someone tips over. You outlast everyone, but your saluting <reading>wrist</reading> locks up stiff, and each hot throb of it beats out <reading>りつ</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: Two people (人) sitting on the earth (土) under a roof.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Anywhere with a <radical>shelter</radical> over it is somewhere two people can <radical>sit</radical>, so that is where they <kanji>sit</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The person who settles onto that patch of earth is Zara, and the moment she sits she lets out a long, satisfied "<reading>ざ</reading>あ" of relief. Every time you see someone plop down here, you hear Zara's ざ.
items.description: Means "sit"; shows up in words about sitting down, seats, and taking a seat.

items.mnemonic_text: A person (人) leaning on a tree (木): resting.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, you spot a <radical>person</radical> slumped sideways against a <radical>tree</radical>, leaning into the trunk like it's the comfiest chair in the world. A <radical>person</radical> plus the tree they're propped against — that's someone taking a well-earned <kanji>rest</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker leaning on that tree lets out a huge, happy sigh — "<reading>きゅう</reading>!" — the sound of every muscle finally letting go. Every time you picture that person melting into rest, you hear that きゅう escape.
items.description: Means "rest" and shows up in everyday words for taking breaks and days off, like 休み.

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth releasing lines of speech: to say.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>words</radical> radical and the <kanji>say</kanji> kanji are the same character, and it reaches past the radical to also mean say, since words only become speech once you say them aloud.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Gen</reading> the parrot repeats whatever you <kanji form="言">say</kanji> <reading>again</reading>, the lines floating up out of his small mouth one by one, each ending in a squawked 「<reading>げん</reading>」.

items.mnemonic_text: A net (罒) over money (貝): buying with cash.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>buy</kanji> a fish you throw a <radical>net</radical> over the whole stall and drop a pile of clam-shell <radical>money</radical> on the counter to haul your catch home.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the fish stall, a sharp-elbowed haggler drags her net of fish to the counter, drops a handful of shells, and waves <reading>bye</reading> to the seller. It comes out as <reading>ばい</reading>, and now nobody at that market can hand over money without blurting <reading>ばい</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: Goods laid out on a stand: selling.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>samurai</radical> too proud to be seen throws a <radical>cover</radical> over his face and takes to the road on his own <radical>human legs</radical>, where the only work left is to <kanji>sell</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The proud samurai hides his face under the cover and trudges the road crying 「<reading>ばい</reading>」, <reading>buy</reading>, buy, since the only work left to him is to <kanji form="売">sell</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: A roof over a heap of good rice: food to eat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>eat</radical> radical and the <kanji>eat</kanji> kanji are one and the same, and food is simply the stuff you eat, so this character carries that sense too.
items.reading_mnemonic: The pointed lid pops off the overstuffed takeout box right in <reading>Shocky</reading>'s face, and after one stunned 「<reading>しょく</reading>」 he grabs his chopsticks and starts to <kanji form="食">eat</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: Food (食) beside a person yawning (欠) for a drink.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A mouth stretched <radical>yawn</radical>-wide beside a flattened tray of <radical>food</radical> is begging for a <kanji>drink</kanji> poured straight in to wash the meal down.
items.reading_mnemonic: A sleepy driver named <reading>Quinn</reading> has just cleared a huge meal at the mountain-trail vending machine, and a jaw-cracking yawn tells him the food left him parched. He feeds in coins and gulps the whole bottle down in one pull, each swallow carrying the same tired groan, <reading>いん</reading>, until the drink is gone.

items.mnemonic_text: A ray of sunlight so bright it turns white.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This <kanji>white</kanji> kanji is nothing new, because it is exactly the <radical>white</radical> radical you already know, in shape and in meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>hawk</reading> swoops down to sip the drop of milk, gets the spark on top right in its beak, and coughs 「<reading>はく</reading>」 as its whole face turns <kanji form="白">white</kanji>.
items.description: Four near-identical boxes. 日 (day or sun) is the plain box with one middle bar and nothing on top. 白 puts a small slanted spark of a stroke above that box. 百 (hundred) is 白 with a full flat line laid over its top. 自 (self) stands taller, with two inner bars instead of one and a short upright nub on top.

items.mnemonic_text: The earth glowing under a big fire: red.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This one comes free, because the <radical>red</radical> radical and the <kanji>red</kanji> kanji are the same character in shape and in meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: The sunburned sprinter finally reaches the riverbank and drops the water <reading>sack</reading> she dragged the whole way, her face still glowing furious red. She's far too parched to speak, so when you ask her name, all that scrapes out is a dry <reading>せき</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: A fresh sprout over the moon: the blue-green of youth.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hold a fresh green <radical>sprout</radical> up against the <radical>moon</radical> and its leaves go the same eerie colour as the moonlit sky, the one shade Japanese calls both <kanji>blue / green</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: After dark on the school sports field, <reading>Sei</reading> holds a sprout up to the moon and lectures you on how its leaves and the sky are one colour. You never asked. That smug little speech, delivered to nobody, is so completely <reading>せい</reading> that the name sticks to the colour for good.
items.description: Japanese long treated blue and green as one colour, and 青 still spans both. A green traffic light is called 青, and unripe fruit or a raw beginner are 青 too. A separate word for green exists now, but 青 keeps the older, wider range.

items.mnemonic_text: A sooty village over a fire: black with smoke.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A whole <radical>village</radical> built right on top of the <radical>fire</radical> pit slowly smokes over until every roof and paddy turns <kanji>black</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Pick through that smoked-out village and the only one still working is a charcoal burner, shovelling black lumps of <reading>coke</reading> into sacks and grunting <reading>こく</reading> with every scoop. His hands, his sacks, and his beard all end up the same sooty <reading>こく</reading> black.

items.mnemonic_text: A tall tower with windows: high and expensive.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the flat <radical>prairie</radical>, a lone tower capped with a pot <radical>lid</radical> and pierced by one <radical>mouth</radical> of a window is the only thing for miles, so it looks impossibly <kanji>tall</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Koichi</reading> the konbini king leans out of the one window of the prairie tower, under its pot-lid roof, and yells 「<reading>こう</reading>」 down at the plain, since nothing for miles stands so <kanji form="高">tall</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) safe under a roof: peaceful and cheap.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>woman</radical> kneeling gracefully inside a snug little house, the <radical>roof</radical> pulled down over her like a blanket. Nothing can reach her in here — she is safe, the rent is nothing, everything is calm. A woman tucked safely under a roof is cheap and <kanji>peaceful</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: She's spreading sweet red <reading>あん</reading> (bean paste) on a bun, humming, utterly at peace. Every bite is cheap comfort — say あん and taste that calm.
items.description: 安 means cheap or peaceful, and shows up in words for low prices, safety, and being at ease.

items.mnemonic_text: A standing tree cut by an axe (斤): freshly new.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take an <radical>axe</radical> to a <radical>tree</radical> that is still <radical>stand</radical>ing and the pale wood you lay bare underneath is perfectly <kanji>new</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Shin</reading> the carpenter sniffs every plank, barks 「<reading>しん</reading>」 at the ones that still smell of sap, and tosses out anything that is not bright and <kanji>new</kanji>.

items.mnemonic_text: Ten (十) mouths (口) of stories passed down: old.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> counts slowly to <radical>ten</radical> every single morning. It has counted so many mornings that the counting itself feels ancient. Something repeated this many times can only be <kanji>old</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every morning Granny <reading>Coco</reading> counts slowly to ten again, croaking 「<reading>こ</reading>」 at each number, a ritual she has repeated so long it is as <kanji form="古">old</kanji> as she is.
items.description: Means "old," as in old and worn from age; appears in words about age and antiquity and in the common word for "used/secondhand."

items.mnemonic_text: Two evenings (夕) stacked: many days piling up.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Set one <radical>evening</radical> on top of another and the stack of spent days behind you already counts as <kanji>many</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Tally</reading> stacks one evening on top of another and marks each with a 「<reading>た</reading>」, until the pile of spent days behind her is far too <kanji form="多">many</kanji> to count.
items.description: The look-alike is 名, meaning name. Both start with the same leaning crescent on top. In this kanji a second identical crescent sits directly below it, the very same shape written twice; in 名 a closed square box sits there instead.

items.mnemonic_text: Small (小) with a slash taken off: even fewer.
items.meaning_mnemonic: One clean <radical>slash</radical> through an already <radical>small</radical> bundle of matchsticks knocks the count down from small to just a <kanji>few</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Sho</reading> the tiny stage magician slashes his wand through a small bundle of matchsticks, shouts 「<reading>しょう</reading>」, and ends his <reading>show</reading> with only a <kanji form="少">few</kanji> left.
items.description: The look-alike 小 means small. 少 is that same shape with one stroke added, a short diagonal cut across the upper right. Cover that top-right stroke and plain 小 remains; the extra slash is the whole difference between small and few.

items.mnemonic_text: Flowing long hair on an elder: long and the eldest.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>long</radical> radical and the <kanji>long</kanji> kanji are the same character, and it also means leader because the one who has served longest is the one everyone follows.
items.reading_mnemonic: The oldest man on the mountain trail has a beard so long it sweeps the path behind him, and everyone bows and calls him Chief <reading>Cho</reading>. Said slowly it stretches into a drawn-out <reading>ちょう</reading>, and that long <reading>ちょう</reading> is how the whole village names the one in charge.

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) already up over the ground (十): early.
items.meaning_mnemonic: It is still <kanji>early</kanji> when the <radical>sun</radical> has climbed only <radical>ten</radical> finger-widths above the hills.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Sew</reading> the tailor holds all ten fingers up against the hills, sees the sun has barely cleared them, and hums <reading>そう</reading> because it is still <kanji form="早">early</kanji>.
items.description: The one kanji covers 'early' in time and 'fast' in pace at once; context, not the character, tells you which sense a sentence means.

items.mnemonic_text: A jewel (玉) enclosed by borders: a country.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>country</kanji> is nothing but an <radical>enclosure</radical> of walls built around the one <radical>jewel</radical> its people refuse to share.
items.reading_mnemonic: The guard <reading>Cook</reading> stands at the one gate in the walls around the jewel, and nobody enters the <kanji form="国">country</kanji> until he slams his stamp down and barks 「<reading>こく</reading>」.

items.mnemonic_text: Drops falling inside a window frame from the sky: rain.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You already know this one, since the <radical>rain</radical> radical you learned and the <kanji>rain</kanji> kanji are the same character down to the last dash.
items.reading_mnemonic: You're pressed to the shrine window watching the rain streak down the glass, and a puddle of it starts to <reading>ooze</reading> under the door across your socks. Grandma Kane's cats line up and stare at the growing puddle, and every one of them lets out the same low, damp <reading>う</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: Rain (雨) with lightning stretching down: electricity.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Electricity</kanji> is nothing but the <radical>lightning</radical> of a <radical>rain</radical> storm, caught and forced to run quietly through your walls instead of splitting the sky.
items.reading_mnemonic: The rain storm is still going when the power cuts out, leaving you in your <reading>den</reading> with one flickering lamp. Each flash outside jolts the lamp bright for a heartbeat, then it fails again. You count the flashes aloud, and every number comes out as the same buzzing <reading>でん</reading>.
items.description: 電 almost never stands on its own; it lives inside compounds. It usually carries the sense of electricity, but by extension it also shortens words for an electric train and for the telephone.

items.mnemonic_text: A cart seen from above with an axle: a vehicle.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>vehicle</radical> radical and this <kanji>car</kanji> kanji are the same character, and it narrows to car because a car is the vehicle almost everyone pictures first.
items.reading_mnemonic: The mechanic <reading>Sasha</reading> greases the long axle under the cart's box body, and each flat wheel she spins hisses <reading>しゃ</reading> until the old cart rolls like a <kanji form="車">car</kanji>.
items.description: The look-alike 重 means heavy. 車 is a tidy sealed box with one vertical line running straight through it and a single bar closing it at top and bottom. 重 is taller, rests a short slanted stroke on top, adds an extra horizontal bar across the body, and lets its centre line push out below the base.

items.mnemonic_text: A horse (馬) waiting where trains stop: a station.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>station</kanji> is where a tired <radical>horse</radical> is swapped for a fresh one, set down every <radical>ruler</radical>-length along the road.
items.reading_mnemonic: The old horse-swap post on the line is a train station now, and its dome is built so the smallest sound comes straight back doubled. The stationmaster murmurs the stop's name once and it <reading>echo</reading>es down the platform as <reading>えき</reading>, loud enough that passengers dozing on the benches sit bolt upright.

items.mnemonic_text: A neck (首) moving down a path: the road and the way.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>road</kanji> is whatever your long <radical>neck</radical> cranes to stare at while your feet <radical>advance</radical>, because you always point your head down the path before you walk it.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Dough</reading> the baker cranes his long neck down the <kanji form="道">road</kanji> before his feet advance a single step, and groans 「<reading>どう</reading>」 at how far his deliveries still have to go.
items.description: Beyond a physical street, 道 also means 'the way' in the sense of a lifelong discipline, which is why it trails the names of pursuits like judo, kendo, and calligraphy.

items.mnemonic_text: A rice field (田) marked out into a town.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>town</kanji> springs up wherever a <radical>street</radical> pushes far enough into the <radical>rice field</radical> that farmers start building shops along both sides of it.
items.reading_mnemonic: A food cart rolls down the new town's one street, and the driver bangs a bell that goes <reading>ちょう</reading> to call the farmers in from the paddies for <reading>chow</reading>. Miss that clang and lunch is gone, so everyone drops their tools the second they hear <reading>ちょう</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: A cloth over a stand where the city market gathers.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>market</kanji> is what you get when every stall hangs out its <radical>cloth</radical> awning and the town claps one <radical>lid</radical> over the whole noisy square.
items.reading_mnemonic: The fishmonger who runs the whole <kanji>market</kanji> is called <reading>Sheena</reading>, and she names her price by slapping a fish on the scale and hissing 「<reading>し</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>father</radical> radical and the <kanji>father</kanji> kanji are the exact same shape and the same word, so this one comes free.
items.reading_mnemonic: Your father stands over the barbecue for a whole hot hour, and when the last plate is full he drops into a chair with a long <reading>ふ</reading> of relief. It is the exact sound a worn-out dad makes, a slow <reading>phew</reading> pushed out through the smoke. The kids know that breath means dinner is finally served.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You already know the <radical>mother</radical> radical, so this <kanji>mother</kanji> kanji is a gift, the same seated figure with both children held tight.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>boa</reading> slides toward the seated woman, so she clutches both children tighter under her arms and gives one low <reading>ぼ</reading>, the warning only a <kanji form="母">mother</kanji> makes.

items.meaning_mnemonic: One stroke <radical>slides</radical> down from the top left across a bar of <radical>ground</radical>, met by a <radical>right hand</radical> rising underneath. Two hands close on each other, nobody paid, nobody in charge: that is a <kanji>friend</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Yuu is always there before you, hand already out. He draws the greeting into a long two-beat call across the car park — 「<reading>ゆう</reading>」 — before you have shut the car door. ゆう means somebody is glad to see you.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Whoever pulls the <radical>arrow</radical> out of you and shuts it inside a <radical>hiding enclosure</radical> has done a <kanji>doctor</kanji>'s entire job.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail a hiker catches a stray arrow graze, and the doctor in the group digs a first-aid kit out of her pack. The moment the antiseptic touches the cut the hiker yelps a sharp <reading>eek</reading>, and it echoes off the rocks as <reading>い</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>employee</kanji> is just one more <radical>mouth</radical> the company has to feed with its own <radical>money</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The paymaster <reading>Inn</reading> drops coins into each open mouth along the company line, grunting <reading>いん</reading> once for every <kanji form="員">employee</kanji> the firm has to feed.
items.description: 員 rarely stands alone as a word for 'employee' — it is a suffix meaning roughly 'a person belonging to,' always riding on a job title, company, or club, closer to '-er' than to a stand-alone noun.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>body</kanji> is the single <radical>book</radical> every <radical>person</radical> is born already holding and can never put down, since each fresh ache is one more page turning itself.
items.reading_mnemonic: Each time a fresh ache turns a page in the book of your <kanji form="体">body</kanji>, the bookbinder <reading>Ty</reading> stitches it into the spine and mutters 「<reading>たい</reading>」 as he pulls it tight.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the farm only the <radical>cow</radical> gets a real name, so every other object that is <radical>not</radical> her is written off as a plain <kanji>thing</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the farm, <reading>Boots</reading> pats the cow by her name but kicks every other <kanji form="物">thing</kanji> out of the barn, spitting 「<reading>ぶつ</reading>」 at each nameless object.

items.meaning_mnemonic: When you quit cooking <radical>food (left)</radical> and do the exact <radical>opposite</radical>, you finally sit down to a proper <kanji>meal</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The moment you stop cooking and sit down instead, <reading>Han</reading> the chef slices your <kanji form="飯">meal</kanji> straight down the middle, since he cannot say 「<reading>はん</reading>」 without halving it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>fish</kanji> is the only animal that will <radical>crouch</radical> in a flooded <radical>rice field</radical> until the water is gone and the <radical>fire</radical> is licking the bottom of the pan.
items.reading_mnemonic: A rockhound in the flooded rice field cracks open a <reading>geode</reading>, and the <kanji form="魚">fish</kanji> crouching beside her leaps up with a startled <reading>ぎょ</reading>, straight into the hot pan.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a steaming cup: delicate <radical>grass</radical> leaves curling up top like visible steam, a little <radical>person</radical> warming his hands round a <radical>tree</radical>-carved cup below. That curling steam over the cup is the whole picture: <kanji>tea</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A dance instructor spins through the tearoom mid cha-cha lesson, a full teacup balanced on his palm. He counts the beat out loud — 「<reading>ちゃ</reading>」-cha-cha — until the cup tips and the lesson ends the same soaked way every time.

items.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>ill</kanji> body is just a healthy one that <radical>sickness</radical> has bumped down to <radical>third class</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The mangy <reading>Bee-Owl</reading>, too <kanji form="病">ill</kanji> to hoot, gets bumped down to a third-class seat and coughs 「<reading>びょう</reading>」 all the way down the carriage.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Raise a truly <radical>perfect</radical> hall high on its own <radical>hill (left)</radical>, and it is grand enough to be called an <kanji>Inst.</kanji>
items.reading_mnemonic: The keeper of the world's biggest <reading>inn</reading> keeps adding wings and halls, yet still bellows 「<reading>いん</reading>」 across a courtyard that has swollen into a full <kanji>Inst.</kanji>
items.description: Short for institution: it names big establishments such as hospitals, temples, and government bodies, and rarely stands alone.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Any <kanji>building</kanji> is just an empty shell until a <radical>bureaucrat</radical> moves in with his stamp and there is enough <radical>food (left)</radical> over from lunch to keep him at the desk.
items.reading_mnemonic: The night caretaker <reading>Khan</reading> clears the bureaucrat's leftover lunch off the desk and snaps 「<reading>かん</reading>」 at anyone still stamping papers in his <kanji form="館">building</kanji> after closing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>cave</radical> that a whole <radical>construction</radical> crew has finished digging out is, for all that effort, still just an <kanji>empty</kanji> hollow in the hill.
